<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|Vireo|6764|virginal}}</noinclude>{{smaller|and sometimes beyond, breeds in all its United States range, and winters from the Southern States to the West Indies and Guatemala. It abounds in shrubbery and tangle, is vivacious and sprightly, has a medley of voluble}}
{{smaller|notes, and hangs its nest in a low bush. Scraps of newspaper usually enter into this fabric, whence the white-eye was nicknamed “the politician” by Wilson. This is one of the longest- and best-known of its family, and was known to the earlier ornithologists as the ''green flycatcher'' (Pennant), ''hanging flycatcher'' (Latham), ''green wren'' (Bartram), etc. White-eyed vireos, like Maryland yellowthroats and summer yellowbirds, are among the most frequent foster-parents of the cowbird. Also called ''white-eyed greenlet.''—'''Yellow-green vireo,''' ''V. flavoviridis'', a near relative of the redeye and whip-tom-kelly, but yellower, of Mexico and over the United States border.—'''Yellow-throated vireo.''' See ''yellow-throated.''}}

[[File:century v08 p0568 c1f1.png|center|274px]]
{{c|{{smaller|White-eyed Vireo (''Vireo noveboracensis'').}}}}

'''Vireonidæ''' (vir-ē̤-on′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Vireo(n-)'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of small dentirostral oscine passerine birds, related to the ''Laniidæ'' or shrikes; the vireos or greenlets. {{smaller|They have a hooked bill, rictal bristles, ten primaries, scutellate tarsi, and toes coherent at the base. They are all small birds, under 7 inches long, of simple and mostly greenish coloration, and are confined to America, where they are migratory in the northern parts. The genera are ''Vireo'', specially characteristic of North America, containing some 30 species in its several sections, with ''Laletes, Cyclarhis, Hylophilus, Vireolanius'', and ''Neochloe'', and probably ''Dulus'' and ''Phœnicomanes. N. brevipennis'' is a Mexican type; ''L. osburni'' is peculiar to Jamaica. The ''Vireonidæ'' are remarkable in possessing either ten, or apparently only nine, primaries in closely related forms, owing to the variable development of the spurious first primary, which is sometimes quite rudimentary. The species of ''Vireo'' are insectivorous, and inhabit woodland and shrubbery, have an earnest and voluble, often highly melodious song, weave pensile nests, and lay spotted eggs. See the phrase-names under ''Vireo'', and cuts under ''Dulus, Hylophilus, redeye, solitary, Vireo'', and ''whip-tom-kelly''.}}

'''Vireoninæ''' (vir″ē̤-ō-nī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Vireo''(''n''-) + ''-inæ''.] The ''Vireonidæ'' rated as a subfamily of ''Laniidæ''.

'''vireonine''' (vir′ē̤-ō-nin), ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the ''Vireonidæ''; resembling or related to a vireo.
{{smaller block|The usual ''Vireonine'' style of architecture . . . a closely-matted cup swung pensile from a forked twig, nearly hemispherical in contour, and rather large for the size of the bird. {{right|''Coues'', Birds of Colorado Valley, I. 523.}}}}

'''Vireosylvia''' (vir″ē̤-ō-sil′vi-ä), ''n.'' [NL. (Bonaparte, 1838), < ''Vireo'' + ''Sylvia'', q. v.] A genus of vireos, or section of ''Vireo'', including the larger greenlets with comparatively slender bill, as the common red-eyed vireo, the black-whiskered vireo, the whip-tom-kelly, and others. See cut under ''greenlet''.

'''virescence''' (vī-res′ens), ''n.'' [< ''virescen''(''t'') + ''-ce''.] '''1.''' Greenness; viridescence.—'''2.''' In ''bot.'', the abnormal assumption of a green color by organs normally bright-colored, as when the petals of a flower retain their characteristic form, but become green.

'''virescent''' (vī-res′ent), ''a.'' [< L. ''virescen(t-)s'', ppr. of ''virescere'', grow green, inceptive of ''virere'', be green: see ''virent''.] Greenish; slightly green; turning or becoming green.

'''vireton†''' (vir′e-ton), ''n.'' [OF. ''vireton'', dim. of ''vire'', a crossbow-bolt: see ''vire''<sup>1</sup>.] Same as ''vire''<sup>1</sup>, 1.

'''virgal''' (vėr′gal), ''a.'' [< L. ''virga'', a rod, twig, + ''-al''.] Made of twigs.

'''virgaloo''', ''n.'' Same as ''virgouleuse''.

'''virgarius''' (vėr-gā′ri-us), ''n.''; pl. ''virgarii'' (-ī). [ML., < L. ''virga'', a rod: see ''verge''<sup>1</sup>, ''virgate''<sup>2</sup>.] The holder of a virgate or yard-land. See ''yard-land''.

'''virgate'''<sup>1</sup> (vėr′gāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''virgatus'', made of twigs, striped, resembling a rod, < ''virga'', a rod, twig: see ''verge''<sup>1</sup>.] Having the shape of a wand or rod; slender, straight, and erect: as, a ''virgate'' stem; a ''virgate'' polyp.

'''virgate'''<sup>2</sup> (vėr′gāt), ''n.'' [< L. ''virga'', a rod, in LL. a measure of land (like E. ''rod'', ''pole'', or ''perch''): see ''verge''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''virgate''<sup>1</sup>.] A measure of surface (corresponding to the ML. ''terra virgata'', called, without much uniformity. Compare quotation under ''holding'', 3 (''a'').

{{smaller block|The half-''virgate'' or bovate [corresponds] with the possession of a single ox. {{right|''Seebohm'', Eng. Vil. Community, p. 65.}}}}

'''virgated''' (vėr′gā-ted), ''a.'' [< ''virgate''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Same as ''virgate''<sup>1</sup>.

'''virget†''', '''virger†'''. Old spellings of ''verge''<sup>1</sup>, ''verger''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Virgilia''' (vėr-jil′i-ä), ''n.'' [NL. (Lamarck, 1793), so called in honor of Virgil (Publius ''Virgilius'' Maro), the Roman poet, with ref. to the botanical interest of his “Georgics.”] A genus of leguminous trees of the tribe ''Sophoreæ.'' {{smaller|It is characterized by papilionaceous rose-purple flowers with a broad banner-petal, falcate wings, and connate keel-petals, and by a sessile ovary which becomes a coriaceous, wingless, flattened two-valved pod. The only species, ''V. Capensis'', is an evergreen tree of Cape Colony, from 15 to 30 feet high, cultivated under the name ''Cape Virgilia;'' it bears pinnate leaves with small leaflets, and handsome flowers in short terminal racemes. ''V. lutea'', the American yellow-wood, is now referred to ''Cladrastis.''}}

'''Virgilian''' (vėr-jil′i-an), ''a.'' [Also ''Vergilian;'' < L. ''Virgilius'' (prop. ''Vergilius'') (see def.) + ''-an''.] '''1.''' Of or pertaining to Virgil (Publius Virgilius Maro), the greatest Roman epic poet (70–19 B. C.): as, the ''Virgilian'' poems.—'''2.''' Resembling the style of Virgil.

{{smaller block|The young candidate for academical honours was no longer required to write Ovidian epistles or ''Virgilian'' pastorals. {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., iii.}}}}

'''virgin''' (vėr′jin), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ME. ''virgine'', ''vergine'', < OF. ''virgine'', vernacularly ''vierge'', F. ''vierge'' = Sp. ''virgen'' = Pg. ''virgem'' = It. ''vergine'', < L. ''virgo'' (''virgin-''), a maid, virgin, girl or woman (in eccl. writers also of males), as adj. unwedded, fresh, unused; root uncertain.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A woman who has had no carnal knowledge of man; a maiden of inviolate chastity; a pure maid. Gen. xxiv. 16.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sure there is a power
In that great name of ''virgin'' that binds fast
All rude uncivil bloods, all appetites
That break their confines.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The decencies to which women are obliged made these ''virgins'' stifle their resentment so far as not to break into open violences. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 80.}}}}
'''2.''' A man who has preserved his chastity.
{{smaller block|These are they which were not defiled with women; for they are ''virgins''. {{right|Rev. xiv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Before the sepulcher of Christ there is masse said euerie day, and none may say the masse there but a man that is a pure ''virgin''. {{right|''E. Webbe'', Travels (ed. Arber), p. 26.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The Saints are ''virgins'';
They love the white rose of virginity; . . .
I have been myself a ''virgin''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Harold, iii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' One who professes perpetual virginity; especially, in the ''early church'', one of a class or order of women who were vowed to lifelong continence.—'''4†.''' The state of virginity.
{{smaller block|St. Jerom affirms that to be continent in the state of widowhood is harder than to keep our ''virgin'' pure. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 90.}}}}
'''5.''' A parthenogenetic insect, as an aphid; a female insect which lays eggs which hatch, though there has been no fecundation for some generations by the male.—'''6.''' Any female animal which has not had young, or has not copulated.—'''7.''' [''cap.''] The zodiacal sign or the constellation Virgo. See ''Virgo.''
{{smaller block|When the bright ''Virgin'' gives the beauteous days.
{{right|''Thomson'', Autumn, l. 23.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Dolors of the Virgin Mary.''' See ''dolor.''—'''English virgins.''' See ''Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary.''—'''Espousals of the Blessed Virgin.''' See ''espousal.''—'''Feast of the Presentation of the Virgin Mary.''' See ''presentation''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Institute of the Blessed Virgin.''' See ''institute.''—'''Little office of the Blessed Virgin.''' See ''office.''—'''Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary.''' See ''nativity.''—'''Order of the Presentation of the Virgin Mary.''' See ''presentation''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Purification of St. Mary the Virgin.''' See ''purification.''—'''Servants of the Holy Virgin.''' See ''Servite.''—'''The Virgin, or the Blessed Virgin,''' the Virgin Mary, the mother of Christ.}}
{{smaller block|This image [that we have conceived] of a beautiful figure with a pleasant expression cannot but have the tendency of afterwards leading us to think of ''the Virgin'' as present when she is not actually present, or as pleased with us when she is not actually pleased.
{{right|''Ruskin'', Lectures on Art, § 50.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Virgin Mary’s cowslip, honeysuckle, milkdrops,''' popular names of the lungwort, ''Pulmonaria officinalis.'' It has spotted leaves, owing, according to a wide-spread tradition, to drops of the Virgin Mary’s milk. ''Britten and Holland.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''Virgin Mary’s nut,''' a tropical nut or bean cast ashore on the western coasts of the British Isles, and popularly considered an amulet against the evil eye. Also called ''snake’s-egg.''—'''Virgin Mary’s thistle,''' properly, the milk-thistle, ''Silybum (Carduus) Marianum''; referred by Halliwell to the blessed thistle, ''Centaurea (Cnicus) benedicta. Britten and Holland.''}}

II. ''a.'' '''1.''' Of or pertaining to a maid or virgin; being a virgin; befitting a virgin; chaste; pure; maidenly; indicating modesty.

{{smaller block|The Day shall come that Men shall see the King of all living Things, and a ''Virgin'' Lady of the World shall hold him in her Lap.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, iv. 43.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''virgin'' captives, with disorder’d charms
(Won by his own, or by Patroclus’s arms),
Rush’d from the tents with cries; and, gath’ring round,
Beat their white breasts, and fainted on the ground.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xviii. 33.}}}}
'''2.''' Unsullied; undefiled: as, ''virgin'' snow; ''virgin'' minds.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''virgin'' Lillie, and the Primrose trew.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Prothalamion, l. 32.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Pardon, goddess of the night,
Those that slew thy ''virgin'' knight.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 3. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>As Phœbus steals his subtil Ray
Through ''virgin'' Crystal. ''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, ii. 110.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Sweet flower, I love, in forest bare,
To meet thee, when thy faint perfume
Alone is in the ''virgin'' air.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Yellow Violet.}}}}
'''3.''' Untouched; not meddled with; unused; untried; fresh; new; unalloyed: as, ''virgin'' soil.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tell him the valour that he shew’d against me
This day, the ''virgin'' valour, and true fire,
Deserves even from an enemy this courtesy.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, ii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Vierge escu, a ''virgin'' shield, or a white shield, without any devices, such as was borne by the tyros in chivalry who had not performed any memorable action.
{{right|''Strutt'', Sports and Pastimes, p. 14, note.}}}}
{{smaller block|Convictions existed in him by divine right; they were ''virgin'', unwrought, the brute metal of decision.
{{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Treasure of Franchard.}}}}

{{smaller block|It is impossible to produce, and at the same time to obtain an account of, what may be called a ''virgin'' sensation, such as may be conceived to be the impression of an infant mind, if indeed even this may be supposed to exist pure from all accretions of transmitted association.
{{right|''J. Sully'', Sensation and Intuition, p. 38.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Sierra Madres in Mexico are still ''virgin'' of sportsmen and skin-hunters. {{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXVIII. 878.}}}}
'''4.''' In ''zoöl.'', parthenogenetic, as an insect; of or pertaining to parthenogenesis: as, ''virgin'' reproduction. See ''agamogenesis''.—{{smaller|'''Virgin birth''' or '''generation''', parthenogenesis.—'''Virgin clay''', in ''industrial arts'', as glass-making and pottery, clay that has never been molded or fired, as distinguished from the ground substance of old ware, which is often mixed with it.—'''Virgin honey.''' See ''honey''.—'''Virgin mercury''', native mercury. See ''mercury''.—'''Virgin oil.''' See ''olive-oil''.—'''Virgin parchment.''' See ''parchment''.—'''Virgin scammony.''' See ''scammony'', 2.—'''Virgin steel''', a deceptive name given to articles made merely of good cast-iron.—'''Virgin stock.''' See ''stock''<sup>1</sup>, 26 (''b'').—'''Virgin swarm''', a swarm of bees from a swarm of the same season. ''Halliwell.''}}

'''virgin''' (vėr′jin), ''v. i.'' [< ''virgin'', ''n.''] To play the virgin; be or continue chaste: sometimes with indefinite ''it''.
{{smaller block|<poem>My true lip
Hath ''virgin’d'' it e’er since. ''Shak.'', Cor., v. 3. 48.</poem>}}

'''virginal<sup>1</sup>''' (vėr′jin-al), ''a.'' [< OF. ''virginal'', ''virgeal'', F. ''virginal'' = Sp. Pg. ''virginal'' = It. ''verginale'', < L. ''virginalis'', maidenly, < ''virgo'' (''virgin-''), a maiden: see ''virgin''.] '''1.''' Pertaining to a virgin; maidenly: as, ''virginal'' reserve.
{{smaller block|With mildnesse ''virginall.'' {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ix. 20.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''virginal'' palms of your daughters.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., v. 2. 45.}}}}

{{smaller block|“Bertha in the Lane” is treasured by the poet’s admirers for its ''virginal'' pathos—the sacred revelation of a dying maiden’s heart.
{{right|''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 129.}}}}

'''2.''' In ''zoöl.'', virgin; parthenogenetic: as, the ''virginal'' reproduction of plant-lice.
